notes.meaning: Arioch, the captain of the guard, rushed Daniel in to see the king. He said, "I have found a man," as if the discovery were his own, even though Daniel had come to him. The commentators say court officials often did this to win the king's favor. He may also have been afraid to admit he had paused the king's order on his own.

The king knew Daniel only by his Babylonian name, Belteshazzar. His question shows amazement and doubt. If all his skilled wise men had failed, could this young captive really do it? The less likely it looked, the more God would get the glory, because God often uses weak and overlooked people.

Daniel first agrees that no human expert could do what the king asked. Daniel had studied their learning himself, so he knew its limits. This dream did not come from nature or human guesswork. Only God could reveal it. Daniel was gently turning the king away from trusting his magicians.

"But there is a God in heaven." Daniel points the king to the true God, unlike the idols men make with their hands. This God reveals secrets. "The latter days" means the future, reaching all the way to the coming of the Messiah (God's promised Savior-King). Before telling the dream, Daniel wisely prepares the proud king to listen.

Before he fell asleep, the king had been wondering what would become of his great empire. God answered those very thoughts in the dream. The king could never have worked out the future by his own thinking. God, the Revealer of Mysteries, had to show him.

Daniel humbly refuses any credit. The secret came to him not because he was smarter than anyone else, but as God's gift, so the king could understand. God's servants in every age point away from themselves to God's grace. God gives his messengers truth so that they will pass it on.

The king saw one huge, shining statue shaped like a man. It was one statue because the world's great empires are really one kind of earthly power, appearing in different forms. It looked splendid to its admirers but terrifying, because these empires would bring fear and suffering to God's people.

The metals drop in value from head to feet: gold, silver, bronze, iron, then iron mixed with clay. The traditional reading sees four empires in a row: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome. The cheaper metals picture the world growing worse over time. The clay is like brittle pottery, so the whole statue stands on weak feet.

A stone cut out "not by human hands" stands for Christ and his kingdom. It comes from God, not from human power or planning. Some older writers also see a hint of Christ's birth without a human father. The stone strikes the weak feet, and the whole statue falls.

Every metal is crushed so fine that it blows away like chaff. Chaff is the light husks blown off grain on an open threshing floor. All human glory passes away like that. But the small stone grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Christ's kingdom starts small and looks humble, then grows beyond all expectation.
Daniel says "we" will tell the meaning. This likely includes his three friends, who had prayed with him for the answer. It shows his modesty. He does not claim the gift for himself alone.

Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold. Gold fits Babylon's great wealth, and it was even called "the golden city." Daniel is careful to say God gave him this power, not his own gods or skill. So this is not flattery. Babylon's greatness was bound up with Nebuchadnezzar himself, though the head of gold also covers his kingdom and the kings after him.

The silver kingdom is Medo-Persia, which followed Babylon. The bronze kingdom is Greece under Alexander the Great, who boasted of ruling the world. "Inferior" may not mean less wealth. It may mean weaker central power, or worse cruelty and pride, as the world sank lower.

The iron kingdom is Rome. It was hard and strong, and it crushed the kingdoms before it, as iron smashes everything. Its strength often showed in harshness and cruelty. In the end, what crushed others would itself be crushed by God's kingdom.

The mix of iron and clay shows a kingdom divided against itself. The commentators point to civil wars and lasting quarrels inside Rome, and to provinces breaking away. Yet some of iron's strength would remain in it.

Like the toes, this kingdom would be partly strong and partly brittle. Many older writers saw the toes as the ten kingdoms that later came out of the Roman world. Some of them were strong as iron and some weak as clay.

"The peoples will mix" points to marriages and alliances meant to make the kingdoms strong. But they never truly bonded, just as iron will not blend with clay. Ambition proved stronger than family ties. Attempts to join the pieces back into one empire failed.

God himself will set up a kingdom that never falls and never passes to another people, unlike every empire before it. This is the kingdom of Christ, which the New Testament calls "the kingdom of heaven." It belongs not only to Christ but to his whole church, which God keeps through every age. Every power that sets itself against Christ will be broken, but his kingdom stands forever.

differ.view: The kingdom began when the gospel was first preached in Roman times. It is mainly spiritual and unseen, and it outlasts and breaks every earthly power that opposes Christ.
The kingdom was set up in the days of Rome and keeps spreading through preaching, Bibles, and missions. It fills the earth bit by bit, never by the sword.
The stone strikes the feet and toes, which did not yet exist when Christ first came. So this is a sudden judgment Christ brings at his second coming, on a final group of ten kings.

notes.meaning: Daniel ends with firm confidence: the dream is true and its meaning is sure. The God who foretold these things has also planned them and will bring them about. Only the true God can tell the future, which idols cannot do. The mountain the stone came from may picture God's heavenly glory, from which Christ came.

The mighty king fell flat before a captive and ordered offerings and incense for him. These were honors meant for a god. Bowing was partly humble, but this worship was wrong, because worship belongs to God alone. The text doesn't say what Daniel did. Most of these commentators think he refused it, as Peter later refused Cornelius, and the text never says the offering was made.

The king praises Daniel's God as "God of gods and Lord of kings," greater than all other gods and ruling over every ruler. These are fine words. But they came from a sudden feeling, not a changed heart. He still kept his other gods, as chapter 3 soon shows.

The king gave Daniel rich gifts and made him governor of the province of Babylon and head of all the wise men. Daniel had not bargained for any reward. He could rightly accept, as Joseph once did in Egypt, because his new position let him help his suffering fellow exiles.

Daniel did not forget his friends, who had prayed with him. He asked that they be given posts in the province. He did this not for their own gain, but so the Jewish captives would be treated more kindly. Daniel himself stayed "at the king's court," serving as one of the king's chief officials.
